As for «He would have made them hear», al-Zajjaj takes it as answering all their questions, Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi as granting them understanding, and al-Mawardi as hearing the dead speak. Al-Razi reads the conditional particle as signifying implication rather than failed condition, while others say the verse denies only the increase of aversion. The commentators do not settle these readings.

In this verse God commands the believers to answer God and His Messenger with obedience when they call them to what gives them life. The commentators differ on what this life is. Al-Suddi understands it as faith, which revives a heart dead in unbelief; Mujahid as the truth; Qatada as the Quran, with its deliverance and protection; Ibn Ishaq as jihad, through which God honoured the Muslims after their humiliation; and al-Qutaybi as martyrdom. Al-Tabari holds that the call means obedience to the Messenger in the truth, which includes fighting, applying the Quran, and everything that gives life to the one who answers, in this world and the next. He cites the report of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, whom the Prophet called while he was praying; Ubayy hastened his prayer and then came. Scholars read this differently: al-Shafi'i holds that answering does not invalidate the prayer, while others say the summons concerned an urgent matter. As for the phrase that God comes between a person and his heart, Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak take it to mean that God separates the believer from unbelief and the unbeliever from faith; Mujahid says it means God takes away a person's reason; al-Suddi, that no one can believe or disbelieve except by God's leave; and Qatada, that God is nearer to a person than his own heart and knows what he conceals. Al-Tabari concludes that the verse states that God holds the hearts of His servants more than they do, and that the wording admits all these meanings. The verse ends by reminding the reader that the return is to God.

God commands the believers to beware of a trial whose effects will not be limited to the wrongdoers among them but will reach everyone when evil goes unchallenged. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Ashur, understand the fitna here as tolerating wrongdoing within the community, since the punishment then covers both the one who commits the sin and the one who accepts it, and they cite the hadith of the ship's passengers and the hadith of Zaynab bint Jahsh. Al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi also report other meanings: a test, division among the people, the wealth and children mentioned elsewhere in the Quran, or the spread of innovations. Regarding the occasion of revelation, al-Hasan, al-Sudi and Qatada connect it with companions involved in the Battle of the Camel, and al-Zubayr himself said the verse concerned them, while Ibn Abbas understood it in general terms. On grammar, al-Farra' treats the negative verb as an answer to the imperative in the sense of a conditional, al-Mubarrad and al-Akhfash treat it as a prohibition after a command or as a supplication, and the reading of Ali and Ibn Mas'ud with the emphatic oath particle is noted. All agree that the verse warns of a widespread trial and calls for upholding what is right, and that God's punishment is severe.

God reminds the believers of His favour when they were few and oppressed in Mecca, fearing that people would snatch them away. He sheltered them, most commentators taking this as the migration to Medina and the support of the Ansar, He strengthened them with His help, chiefly at Badr, and He provided them with good things, which are the spoils of war, so that they would give thanks. The commentators differ on who the people they feared were. Ibn Abbas, Ikrima, Qatada and Ibn Kathir name the Quraysh or the pagan Arabs. Al-Tabari adopts this reading, reasoning that the Muslims before the hijra feared no one but the Quraysh, being closest to them and most hostile. Wahb ibn Munabbih names Persia and Byzantium, an opinion followed by several exegetes, while Qatada describes the humbled Arabs of that time between the two empires. As for the shelter, most read it as the hijra and the Ansar's welcome, whereas al-Mawardi takes it as a secure dwelling place. The support is Badr for most, though some say angels or Ansar aid. Zamakhshari and Razi note that spoils, forbidden to earlier nations, were made lawful for this community. Ibn Juzayy holds that the address is to the Arabs at large, while Ibn Ashur and al-Qasimi argue it is to the emigrants alone, which suits the context better. All agree on the closing call to gratitude, and that the believers' honour came through Islam.

In this verse God forbids the believers to betray God and His Messenger, or the trusts placed in them, and reminds them that they know the gravity of such betrayal. The commentators explain that betraying God and the Messenger means neglecting the obligations and the Sunna, showing obedience while hiding disobedience, or embezzling from the spoils of war. The trusts (amanat) are understood as what God has entrusted to His servants, namely their religious duties, and according to some, all that people hold in trust. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others report that the verse was revealed concerning Abu Lubaba ibn Abd al-Mundhir, who gestured to the Banu Qurayza that they would be slaughtered. Other reports link it to a man who wrote to Abu Sufyan to warn him, to Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a, or to the killing of Uthman. Al-Tabari concluded that the verse may have been revealed about Abu Lubaba or about someone else, without deciding between them. Ibn Kathir and Ibn Ashur stress that the general wording governs, not the particular occasion. All agree that betrayal means diminishing or concealing, the opposite of faithfulness. On grammar, most treat the second verb as a continuation of the prohibition in the jussive, while al-Baydawi also allows the subjunctive as a response to the prohibition, and Mujahid read the singular form amanatakum. Al-Razi takes the phrase 'while you know' to mean that the betrayal is deliberate rather than an oversight, while others take it to mean knowing the ugliness of the act; Ibn Ashur sees it as an emphatic clause. The next verse explains that wealth and children are a trial that tempts one to betrayal, and that a great reward is with God.

The commentators explain that God addresses the believers, telling them that their wealth and children are a trial through which He tests them, to see whether they will be grateful and obedient or will be distracted from Him. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand fitna as a test, while al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi also see it as something that can lead to sin or punishment. All agree that the great reward with God is better than wealth and children, so one should prefer His pleasure to the accumulation of property and excessive love for offspring.

Most link the verse to the episode of Abu Lubaba, who, out of concern for his property and children held by the Banu Qurayza, signalled to them by a gesture of the throat that they would be slaughtered if they surrendered, as reported by al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Ashur. Ibn Kathir and al-Razi note, however, that the general wording of the verse is what matters rather than the particular occasion. Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Ashur hold that the warning covers every hidden betrayal, including misappropriation of spoils. Others, such as al-Mawardi and al-Razi, report that betraying God and His Messenger may mean disobeying their commands, revealing secrets or neglecting the duties entrusted to one. Sayyid Qutb, Ibn Sa'di and al-Sha'rawi stress the trial character of wealth and children and the choice between divine reward and worldly attachment.

This verse promises the believers who are mindful of God three things: God will give them a furqan, a criterion by which to tell truth from falsehood, He will remove their bad deeds, and He will forgive them, and He is the Lord of immense bounty. The commentators differ on the meaning of furqan. Mujahid, Ikrima, al-Dahhak and, in one report, Ibn Abbas take it as a way out of hardship and doubt; al-Suddi and Qatada take it as deliverance; al-Farra' and, in another report, Ibn Abbas take it as victory; Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Zayd take it as the separation of truth from falsehood and a guidance placed in the heart. Al-Tabari holds that these meanings are close to one another, and Ibn Kathir combines them by saying that piety entails all of them. Al-Razi and al-Nasafi understand furqan to include inner guidance, the opening of the heart, and the believers' triumph in this world and their reward in the next. Al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi report several meanings without preferring one. On the bad deeds and sins, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Sa'di distinguish minor offences from major ones, while al-Alusi and Ibn Ashur take the concealment to be in this world and the absence of punishment in the next. Several exegetes report that the verse was revealed concerning the betrayal of Abu Lubaba, and Ibn Atiyya also links betrayal to the killing of 'Uthman. Al-Razi argues that God's grace surpasses that of anyone else, since He seeks no return and needs no one.

This verse recalls God's favour upon His Prophet ﷺ when the leaders of Quraysh plotted against him in the Assembly House: to imprison him in bonds, to kill him, or to expel him from Mecca. The commentators explain "to confine you" in several ways: to bind and shackle him, to imprison him, or to wound him severely. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report these meanings and note that they converge on depriving him of freedom of movement, while other readings such as "to lodge you" or "to fetter you" are also cited.

As for "and Allah plots," most exegetes take it to mean that God frustrates their scheme and turns it back upon them, and that He is the best of schemers. Al-Zamakhshari sees here a figure of speech by which the word is used for God's own response, while al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi stress that God's plotting is more effective than theirs. Ibn 'Ashur observes that the present tense evokes the scene of the plot as it unfolded.

The commentators agree on the setting: the group's final resolution was to strike the Prophet with a single blow of swords, carried out by young men from every clan so that his blood would be spread among the tribes. God then informed His Prophet, who left Mecca for the Hijra while 'Ali slept in his bed. Detailed accounts of these events appear in Ibn Ishaq, al-Tabari and al-Baghawi. Al-Razi discusses the form Iblis took, but most commentators relate the story without questioning it.

Opinions differ on when the verse was revealed: Ibn Kathir, al-Tabari and Ibn 'Ashur consider it Medinan, whereas 'Ikrima and Mujahid call it Meccan. Ibn Kathir notes that the plot itself took place before the Hijra and was recalled in revelation at Medina.

This verse reports how the disbelievers reacted when the verses of the Qur'an were recited to them: they claimed to have heard them and said that, if they wished, they could produce something similar, adding that this is nothing but the fables of the ancients. Most commentators, beginning with al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Wahidi and al-Baghawi, report that the speaker was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who traveled to Persia and Hira, brought back the tales of Persian kings and the stories of Christians, and was taken prisoner by al-Miqdad at Badr and then executed. Ibn Kathir describes the statement as pure falsehood. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn Ashur see it as vanity and arrogance, since they had been challenged and never met the challenge. Al-Razi explains that the particle "law" (if) implies that the act did not happen: they neither willed nor said it. The general meaning is therefore shared: inability before the challenge to imitate the Qur'an, and resort to denial. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi note that the plural pronoun may express a leader's words attributed to the group, and Abu Hayyan, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud make the same point. The differences concern mainly the identity of the speaker and how the claim to be able to imitate the Qur'an should be understood, not the general sense of the verse.

This verse reports the prayer of the Quraysh who said: O God, if what Muhammad brings is the truth from You, then rain down stones upon us from the sky or bring us a painful punishment. The sense is a vehement denial: they assert that the Qur'an is false and call for punishment for rejecting it, tying the penalty to something they regard as impossible. The commentators differ on who spoke these words. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi and Ibn Atiyya attribute it, at least in part, to al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, according to transmissions from Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi, while al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir also report from Anas, in al-Bukhari, that it was Abu Jahl; others say it was the Quraysh as a group. On the particle huwa, the Basran grammarians treat it as a separating pronoun and the Kufans as a supporting element; the common reading puts al-haqq in the accusative, and al-A'mash read it in the nominative. For the next verse, most hold that God does not punish them while the Prophet is among them. Scholars differ on istighfar: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Ikrima explain it as seeking forgiveness or accepting Islam, al-Tabari and al-Zamakhshari take it as a condition, and Abu Musa transmitted the hadith of the two protections. All agree that their obstruction of the Sacred Mosque was a cause for punishment, and that God's true allies are the righteous. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Juzayy consider that their aim was to clear themselves of blame rather than to invoke a curse upon themselves.

This verse states that God did not send a total punishment upon the Quraysh while the Prophet ﷺ was among them, and that seeking forgiveness also protected them. The commentators place it in the context of the pagans asking for an immediate punishment: "O God, if this is the truth from You, rain down stones upon us from the sky." Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, citing Ibn Abbas, Abu Malik and al-Dahhak, read "those who seek forgiveness" as the believers who remained in Mecca. In this view the punishment came only after they left, at Badr or at the conquest of Mecca. Others, including Ibn Abbas, Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and Ikrimah in one report, take the istighfar to be the pagans' words during the circumambulation, "Forgive us, our Lord." Mujahid and Ikrimah interpret it as Islam, and Mujahid also takes it as referring to descendants who would later believe. Qatadah, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd understand that had they sought forgiveness they would not have been punished. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi discuss the grammar of the lam and the sense of the clause as a circumstance. Al-Tabari rejects the claim that the verse was abrogated, since a statement of fact cannot be abrogated, a view shared by Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Atiyya. The hadith from Abu Musa about the two protections, the Prophet and istighfar, is reported by al-Tirmidhi, who judged it weak. Ibn Kathir also cites hadiths on the value of seeking forgiveness. The general meaning remains that the Prophet's presence and the seeking of forgiveness held back the punishment.

This verse says that God would not punish the polytheists while the Prophet ﷺ was among them, nor while they asked forgiveness, yet it also states that they deserve punishment because they bar the believers from the Sacred Mosque. Their claim to guard it is rejected, since only the God-fearing are its true protectors, though most of them do not know this. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi agree on this general sense, and that the Sacred Mosque here means being prevented from circumambulating and praying there. The meaning of the seeking of forgiveness is disputed. Ibn Abbas, Abu Malik and al-Dahhak take it to mean the forgiveness sought by believers who remained in Mecca, while Qatada and al-Sudi understand it as a condition: had they asked forgiveness, they would not have been punished. Mujahid and Ikrima take it to mean embracing Islam, and Mujahid and Ibn Abbas also link it to prayer. The punishment that was lifted is also variously identified: some say it is total destruction, others the punishment at Badr, and others the punishment of the Hereafter. Al-Hasan and Ikrima consider the first statement abrogated by the second, but al-Tabari and al-Nahhas reject this because a report cannot be abrogated. On the words mukaa' and tasdiya, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Umar and Mujahid explain them as whistling and hand-clapping performed around the Ka'ba, which Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report as a mockery intended to disrupt the Prophet's prayer.

This verse states that the prayer of the polytheists at the Sacred House was not real prayer but only whistling and hand-clapping. The commentators explain that mukaa' means whistling and tasdiya means clapping. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Dahhak and most exegetes agree on this meaning. Several report that the Quraysh circled the Ka'ba naked, whistling and clapping, and that men stood to the right and left of the Prophet during his prayer to confuse his recitation, a account given by Mujahid and Muqatil. Al-Tabari, al-Mawardi, Ibn Kathir and others repeat these explanations, some adding that the men put their fingers in their mouths. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn Zayd take tasdiya to mean barring people from the House or from the path of God. Al-Tabari finds this reading linguistically unsound, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya derive the word from the echo (sada) or from the verb meaning to obstruct, with one letter changed. On the word salat, al-Mawardi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Razi offer two answers: these acts stood in place of prayer in the polytheists' own view, or the verse uses a figure of speech where one whose practice is this has no prayer at all. The phrase 'taste the punishment' is taken by most to mean the killing and capture at Badr, while some apply it to the Hereafter. Al-Tabari rejects the claim that the preceding verse was abrogated by this one.

This verse says that those who disbelieved spend their wealth to turn people away from the path of God, meaning His religion and following His messenger. This spending will turn against them, becoming a source of regret and anguish, because their wealth will be lost without their reaching what they hoped for, namely extinguishing God's light. They will then be defeated, and those who remained in disbelief will be gathered toward Hell. The commentators differ on who is meant. Ibn Abbas, al-Kalbi and Muqatil identify the twelve leading men of Quraysh who fed the army at Badr, each slaughtering ten camels a day. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Ibn Abza and al-Sudi apply it to Abu Sufyan, who hired two thousand Ahabish at Uhud and spent forty ounces of gold on them. Al-Dahhak refers it to the people of Badr in general, while Ibn Ishaq links it to those who gathered money from the caravan after Badr to fight the Prophet. Al-Tabari concludes that the verse broadly addresses those who funded the war against the Prophet, and Ibn Kathir holds that, although its cause was specific, its meaning is general. Commentators also note that the clause about God distinguishing the wicked from the good is attached by some to the gathering into Hell and by others to the regret, so that the distinction concerns bad and good expenditures.

The verse says that the disbelievers spend their wealth to turn people away from God's path, that this spending will become a source of regret for them, and that they will then be overcome. God will separate the wicked from the good, heaping the wicked together in a pile and casting it into Hell; those are the losers. The commentators agree that those gathered to Hell are the disbelievers, and that the wicked and the good usually refer to the disbeliever and the believer. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi and Muqatil extend the separation to the people of happiness and the people of misery. On the occasion of revelation they differ: Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibn Abza and al-Hakam ibn 'Utayba link it to Abu Sufyan's spending at Uhud, Muqatil and al-Kalbi to those who fed the army at Badr, and al-Dahhak to the people of Badr. Ibn Ishaq recounts how Quraysh gathered money after Badr. Al-Zamakhshari and others suggest the wicked may be the wealth spent by the polytheists and the good the wealth spent by the Muslims, such as Abu Bakr and 'Uthman, and that the lam then attaches to the regret or defeat rather than to the gathering, which most commentators attach to the gathering. Ibn 'Atiyya and others add that the wicked may mean wealth whose zakat was not paid, and Ibn Kathir notes that the verse is general even if its cause is specific. Al-Hasan reports that hoarded wealth will be heated in Hell, as in the verse of repentance. On the reading, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read the doubled form, while the others read the single form; Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred the doubled form.

God tells His Prophet to say to those who disbelieve, namely the Quraysh and above all Abu Sufyan and his companions, that if they desist from unbelief and from hostility and fighting, their past sins will be forgiven; but if they return to fighting, the way of the earlier peoples has already passed. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, following Mujahid, understand the warning as aimed at the Quraysh of Badr and other earlier nations, while al-Suddi and Ibn Ishaq take it as referring to the fate of those killed at Badr. On the meaning of desisting, many commentators take it as ceasing hostility and war, whereas Ibn Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi take it as ceasing disbelief itself, since forgiveness of past sins applies only to one who has given up unbelief. Al-Mawardi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir cite the sound hadith that Islam wipes out what came before it to support the view that conversion erases past offences. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya explain that returning means returning to fighting rather than to disbelief, since these people had never left unbelief. Jurists drew rulings from the verse on what a disbeliever or apostate owes once he embraces Islam: Malik holds that acts committed in unbelief, such as divorces and oaths, are dropped, but not the rights of people; Abu Hanifa holds that only the rights of God are dropped; al-Shafi'i, according to the reports cited by Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn al-Arabi, holds that all rights remain owed, and the scholars differ. Al-Razi also uses the verse to argue that the repentance of a heretic is accepted, which Malik rejects.

This verse commands the believers to fight the disbelievers until there is no shirk and no religious persecution, and until religion belongs entirely to God. If they desist, God sees what they do and will reward them. Most commentators take fitna to mean polytheism: Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Suddi and al-Tabari all say so, and al-Tabari adds that the aim is for worship and obedience to belong to God alone. Ibn Kathir reports that this means the testimony that there is no god but God must be affirmed. Ibn Ishaq, al-Zamakhshari and others understand fitna also as the persecution of believers for their faith, as the Quraysh inflicted on converts, which Ibn Kathir links to the migration to Abyssinia and then to Medina. Ibn 'Umar holds that this was already fulfilled in the Prophet's time, when Islam had spread, and he rejects the idea that fighting for power falls under this verse. Al-Hasan gives fitna the general sense of trial. Al-Tabari, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya read the phrase 'if they desist' as giving up disbelief and entering Islam; al-Tabari argues that fighting must continue until they convert, since ceasing hostilities alone is not enough. Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Jalalayn take it simply as giving up disbelief. Some commentators connect the verse to the rule that Islam erases what came before it. Some readers recite 'what you do', addressing the fighters directly. The commentators do not settle these differences.

The commentators explain that this verse closes the preceding passage, which calls the disbelievers to give up their unbelief and their fighting against the believers. Its meaning is that if the disbelievers turn away from faith and persist in war, the believers must be certain that God is their protector, their helper and their supporter, for He is the best of protectors and the best of helpers. Al-Tabari explains that this means God's aid against the idolaters and the victory that follows, while Ibn Ishaq and al-Suddi report that this help refers to the victory at Badr, when God honoured the Muslims despite their small number. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi explain that whoever God takes as protector is not lost, and whoever God supports cannot be defeated. Ibn Sa'di sees in it a protection that defeats the schemes of the wicked, while al-Razi and Ibn Kathir read a promise of guardianship and sufficiency. Al-Sha'rawi stresses that divine support, unlike any human ally, neither dies nor weakens. Most agree in understanding the wilaya as support and assistance, and in holding that victory comes from God and not from numbers, without any of them condemning another's reading.

This verse sets out how spoils of war are divided. God tells the believers that whatever they seize from the unbelievers by force belongs one-fifth to God, to the Messenger, to the near kin, to orphans, to the needy and to the wayfarer, while the remaining four-fifths go to the fighters. Most commentators explain that the word "God" opens the statement as a blessing and glorification, since everything belongs to God, and that God's share and the Messenger's share are one, as transmitted from Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i. Abu al-Aliya held that the fifth is divided into six, with one part for the Ka'ba, a view most others regard as exceptional. Al-Shafi'i and most jurists divide the fifth into five and assign the Messenger's share, after his death, to the general interests of the Muslims, whereas Abu Hanifa holds that the shares of the Messenger and the near kin lapse at his death and the fifth goes to the remaining three categories, while Malik leaves the matter to the ruler's judgement. As for the near kin, Mujahid and Ali ibn al-Husayn name the Banu Hashim, al-Shafi'i adds the Banu al-Muttalib, and others take the whole of Quraysh, as Ibn Abbas reported. The orphan is a child who has lost his father, the needy is one who lacks sufficiency, and the traveller is one cut off from his means. Al-Tabari reads the condition of faith as acknowledging God's oneness and what was revealed on the Day of the Criterion, the day of Badr, when the two hosts met. The commentators report many accounts about the division and the battle, but all agree that victory comes from God, who is powerful over all things.

The verse describes the positions at Badr: the Muslims stood on the nearer bank of the valley, toward Medina, while the polytheists camped on the farther bank, toward Mecca, and the caravan of Abu Sufyan passed lower down, nearer the sea. Neither side knew where the other was until they met. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Qurtubi agree that God brought the two armies together without any prior appointment, so that He might accomplish a matter already decreed: the victory of His friends and the humbling of His enemies. Had they arranged a meeting, they would have disagreed about its time, given the enemy's greater numbers. Al-Tabari and Ibn Ishaq state the purpose as follows: whoever perished would do so after a clear proof, and whoever lived would live after a clear proof. Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Atiyya read the words 'perish' and 'live' as metaphors for disbelief and faith, while al-Tabari takes them literally as death and survival. Al-Razi, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi mention both readings. The recitations differ on 'al-'idwa': most read it with a 'u' vowel, while Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it with an 'i', and the commentators treat both as the same word. All stress God's favour in the event and that He hears and knows everything.

This verse describes a dream the Prophet ﷺ had, in which God showed him the enemy as few in number. He told his companions, and their hearts were strengthened. Had God shown them to him as many, the believers would have lost heart and quarrelled over what to do, but God preserved them from this, for He knows what the breasts conceal. The commentators broadly agree that the dream steadied and encouraged the believers. Al-Tabari, Mujahid, Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Jalalayn report that it was a reassurance to them. Several, including al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Ashur, explain that the smallness in the dream stood for the weakness of the enemy rather than an exact count. The meaning of "fashila" and "tanazaʿtum" is debated: al-Tabari links them to cowardice and backing down, while al-Razi, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi understand them as disagreement between standing firm and fleeing. Al-Hasan al-Basri held that "in your sleep" means "in your eye", since the eye is where sleep occurs, which would make the sight a waking one; al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi regard this reading as weak. As for "salama", al-Tabari takes it to mean that God secured the victory for the believers, while Ibn Atiyya gives it a broader sense of protection from every threat that worried them.

This verse recalls a favour of God on the day of Badr: each side was made to see the other as small in number. The believers were shown the enemy as few so that they would advance against them, and the disbelievers were shown the believers as few so that they would not prepare themselves. Once the fighting began, God made the disbelievers see the believers as twice their number, which struck them with dismay. The commentators link this to the true dream the Prophet ﷺ had beforehand, which prepared the believers. They agree that the purpose of this divine arrangement was that a decreed matter be accomplished, namely the victory of Islam, the honour of its people and the humbling of polytheism, and that all affairs return to God. They differ on the nature of the sight. Mujahid, Ibn Ishaq and most exegetes, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, take it to be a dream, while al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that al-Hasan understood it as a waking vision, a view az-Zamakhshari considers poorly supported. Ibn 'Atiyya argues that the Prophet already knew the enemy's numbers. Az-Zamakhshari, an-Nasafi and al-Alusi explain that God could hide part of a crowd or alter the eye, as the squinting man sees one thing as two, whereas al-Razi notes the Mu'tazili explanations. Ibn 'Ashur sees in these perceptions a deliberate error willed by God to secure victory, and Ibn Kathir concludes the two verses reconcile: the small number appeared at the encounter, the large number after the battle was joined.

In this verse God commands the believers to stand firm when they meet a group of disbelievers in battle, and to remember God often, asking Him for victory, so that they may prosper. The commentators agree that steadfastness means not fleeing and holding one's ground, and that abundant remembrance includes supplication and reliance on God. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report Qatada's view that God made His remembrance obligatory at the moment of greatest preoccupation, the clash of swords, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi understand it as turning wholly to God and trusting Him. Some explain that remembrance should be both in the heart and on the tongue, others that it means asking for help, and others that it means glorifying God and calling down defeat on the enemy. There is disagreement about raising the voice: most advise against it for an individual fighter, while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi consider it praiseworthy when all shout together during the charge, since it weakens the enemy. The verse is linked to what follows, the command to obey and avoid dispute. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi take 'wind' to mean power or dominion, whereas Qatada and Ibn Zayd understand a wind sent by God for victory. Most commentators take 'prosper' to mean attaining one's aim of victory and reward.

In this verse God commands the believers to obey Him and His Messenger, and forbids them from disputing, for dispute breeds weakness and cowardice and causes their strength and prestige to vanish. He then commands them to be patient and promises that God is with those who persevere, by His help and support. The commentators agree that dispute means differing in opinion and dividing the ranks, and that failure (fashl) means cowardice and holding back from fighting. As for the word rih, usually rendered 'wind' or 'breath', al-Tabari, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and Qatada take it to mean the wind of victory sent by God to strike the enemy's faces, citing the hadith: 'I was given victory by the east wind and the people of 'Ad were destroyed by the west wind'. Al-Akhfash, Abu 'Ubayda and Ibn Qutayba understand it as dominion or power, while others mention awe or vigour. Ibn 'Atiyya holds that dispute removes this strength only when the enemy knows of it, whereas Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di keep the general sense of strength and force. On patience there is broad agreement that it is the greatest cause of victory and that God's presence means His help and support. Ibn al-Qayyim expands at length on the virtue of patience, citing many verses.

This verse warns believers not to imitate the pagans who marched out of their homes with insolence (batar), meaning arrogance that forgets the blessings one has received, and to show off (riya') before people, while turning others away from the path of God. The commentators agree that the verse refers to the Quraysh at the battle of Badr, who had set out to protect their caravan. When Abu Sufyan told them the caravan was safe and urged them to turn back, Abu Jahl refused and insisted on reaching Badr, where they planned to drink wine, listen to singing girls and make the Arabs talk of them. Instead they were given the cups of death in place of wine. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Mujahid take the verse as a call to sincerity, doing deeds for God alone and not seeking the praise of people. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya understand it as a warning against the same conduct that led to defeat, and as applying to anyone who acts the same way. Al-Razi defines riya' as wanting to display good while hiding what is bad, and distinguishes it from hypocrisy, which is professing faith while concealing disbelief. Al-Qurtubi and al-Nasafi explain batar as a state in which an abundance of blessings keeps a person from being grateful for them. The verse ends by stating that God encompasses what people do, meaning that He knows it fully and will hold them to account for it.

This verse recalls a scene from the battle of Badr, when Satan made the disbelievers' deeds appear fair to them, assuring them that no one among men would defeat them and that he would protect them. The commentators agree that Satan deceived them and made falsehood appealing. They differ on how this happened. Al-Hasan and al-Asamm take it as an inner whispering without any human form. Ibn Abbas, Ibn Ishaq, al-Suddi and al-Kalbi, followed by Ibn Kathir, report that he appeared as Suraqa ibn Malik al-Mudlaji of Kinana, at a time when Quraysh feared Banu Bakr. All agree that he withdrew when he saw the angels descend to help the believers, disowning the polytheists and saying: I see what you do not see, I fear Allah. Qatada and Ibn Ishaq read this as a lying claim, since he had no fear of God, while al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Anbari hold that he feared that his appointed term had come, and al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan say he feared for himself. On the closing phrase, some attribute it to Satan's speech and others take it as God's own statement. Several cite the Muwatta hadith on Satan's humiliation at Badr, noting its weak chain, and some modern scholars avoid detailing these unseen events.

This verse describes two groups of people whose faith was weak: the hypocrites, and those with a sickness in their hearts. Seeing how few the Muslims were compared with their enemy, they said: "Their religion has deluded these people", meaning that their faith had led them into a fight they could not possibly sustain. The commentators offer several closely related readings. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Sha'bi and Ibn Jurayj identify the speakers as men of Mecca who had professed Islam without migrating, and who went out with the polytheists to Badr; Mujahid names several of them. Al-Hasan holds that the speakers were the polytheists themselves. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and Ibn 'Atiyya understand both descriptions as applying to one group, those who were not firm in Islam. Ibn 'Ashur explains that "delusion" is used figuratively here, meaning harm brought about by a false promise of benefit.

All the commentators agree on the divine answer: "Whoever relies upon Allah, then Allah is Mighty and Wise." Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that whoever entrusts his affair to God is guarded and helped, because God is almighty and cannot be overcome, and wise in His dealings. They note that the command was addressed to the Companions of the Prophet and to the other believers. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan read the reply as a rejection of the claim that religion itself causes deception: it is trust in God that brings victory.

Opinions also differ on when the remark was made. Some place it at the moment the two armies met, others at the time of departure. Ibn Juzayy and al-Jalalayn take it to be words spoken at Badr, while al-Razi notes that they may have been said in Medina before the fighters set out.

God tells His Prophet ﷺ that if he could witness the moment the angels take the souls of the disbelievers, striking their faces and their backs and saying: taste the punishment of the burning fire, he would see a dreadful sight. The commentators agree on the general meaning: the verse depicts the torment and ruin of the unbelievers. They differ on the time and the precise reference. Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Juraij, followed by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, say it refers to those killed at Badr, though Ibn Kathir adds that its scope covers every unbeliever. Muqatil, al-Mawardi and others take tawaffi to mean death itself, so the striking happens at the moment of dying or on the Day of Resurrection. Some say the angels strike with whips of fire. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir cite the report of the man who saw a mark like a sandal strap on the back of Abu Jahl, which Ibn Kathir judges to be mursal. As for the backs, most scholars take it to mean the buttocks, which God names with discretion; others, including al-Tabari and al-Baydawi, take it as the front and back of the body. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi distinguish the face turned toward the enemy from the back of those fleeing. All link the punishment to sins, and Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di stress that God does not wrong anyone. The answer to 'if' is left implicit for effect, and the word 'taste' is preceded by an implied verb of speech whose speaker is debated.

This verse describes what unbelievers undergo at death, or on the day of Badr according to some commentators, when the angels strike their faces and backs and say: taste the burning punishment. Most commentators take the backs (adbar) to mean the buttocks, with God using a euphemism; Ibn Abbas understood them as the backs. Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ibn Jurayj read the faces and backs as the whole body, meaning the blows cover everything. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note the scene may happen at death or on the Day of Resurrection as they are driven to the Fire. Az-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi treat the scene as a circumstance of the angels at the moment of taking souls. As for the phrase 'because of what your hands have sent forth', all agree it means the disbelief and sins they committed; al-Razi notes that the hand here stands for power and action. The clause 'God is not unjust to His servants' is read by all as an affirmation of divine justice. Az-Zamakhshari and Ibn Kathir see an intensive form meaning extreme oppression or a denial of any oppression, and al-Baydawi stresses that punishment follows sins and not an arbitrary harm, while Ibn 'Ashur finds the Mu'tazili reading overstated, since leaving a fault unpunished is not injustice. The commentators link the verse to the mention of Pharaoh's people and earlier nations, and to God's rule that He does not change a blessing until people change what is within themselves.

This verse states that the conduct of the Quraysh slain at Badr resembles that of the people of Pharaoh and the nations before them: they rejected God's signs, so God seized them for their sins, for He is mighty and severe in punishment. The commentators agree that the word "dab" means habit or constant practice. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that God's dealings with disbelievers follow a single pattern, while Ibn 'Abbas adds that Pharaoh's people had recognised Moses as a prophet before denying him, and that the Quraysh did the same with the Prophet. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi read the clause about rejecting God's signs as an explanation of this conduct. Al-Zamakhshari also argues that God does not alter a blessing given to a people until they change their own state, and holds that the Quraysh made their condition worse. Ibn 'Atiyya sees the verse as an expression of wonder at what befell the disbelievers at Badr and as a warning to those who remain, and notes that the dab may refer to God's custom with peoples in general. Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan discuss the meanings of the angels striking faces and backs, either at death or at Badr. Ibn 'Ashur and al-Alusi note that the emphatic wording and the adjective "strong" serve as a threat to the polytheists. Ibn Sa'di concludes that this is God's enduring way with earlier and later peoples.

This verse explains that the destruction that struck the disbelievers of Quraysh at Badr was a consequence of their disbelief, and that God does not withdraw a blessing He has granted to a people until that people changes what is within themselves, moving from gratitude and obedience to ingratitude and disobedience. The commentators agree on this general meaning. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and others hold that God does not alter His favours on His own initiative but responds to people's change of conduct. They differ on what the blessing is. Al-Suddi, followed by al-Tabari, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir, identifies it as the mission of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, which Quraysh rejected and which was transferred to the Ansar; al-Kalbi and Muqatil take it to mean being fed after hunger and secured after fear. Al-Mawardi offers several readings, including victory, protection from enemies, wealth, reward or guidance. Al-Zamakhshari, followed by al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud, describes the change as a move from an acceptable state to a worse one. Ibn al-Qayyim and Ibn Sa'di draw the lesson that sins remove blessings. Al-Razi explains that God's action does not depend on human acts and that His decree comes first, and he reads the wrongdoing as disbelief and disobedience. Ibn 'Atiyya links the passage to the Banu Qurayza but holds that it applies to anyone who shares their conduct.

This verse likens the conduct of the Quraysh, who denied the signs of their Lord, to that of the people of Pharaoh and the nations before them. God destroyed them for their sins, drowned the people of Pharaoh, and all of them were wrongdoers against themselves. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi take this as a comparison of persistent denial of the messengers and the punishment that followed; al-Tabari also applies it to those killed at Badr. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi read the second comparison as one of changing a state: just as Pharaoh's people altered God's favour by their disbelief, God altered their condition through punishment. Ibn 'Atiyya links this to God's favour to the Quraysh in the person of the Prophet, which they rejected and which was transferred to the Ansar, a view also reported from al-Suddi.

Al-Razi distinguishes the two clauses: the first concerns denial of divine proofs, the second denial of the blessings of lordship, and the repetition serves emphasis or detail. Al-Qurtubi holds that it is not a repetition, since the first refers to the habit of denial and the second to the habit of changing blessings. Most commentators agree that God does not change a blessing given to a people until they change what is within themselves, moving from obedience to disobedience, and they see this as part of His justice. Al-Jaza'iri and Ibn Sa'di add that the rule applies to all nations, and that God is not unjust when He punishes those who wrong themselves.

This verse states that in Allah's sight the worst of creatures that move on the earth are those who persist in disbelief and become firmly entrenched in it, so that faith cannot be expected from them. The commentators agree that this description refers to the Jews of the Banu Qurayza, and according to some reports to Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and his companions. The Prophet had made a covenant with them not to aid anyone against him, but they broke it by arming the Meccan polytheists, then excused themselves by claiming forgetfulness and error, and broke it again at the Battle of the Trench. Al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi report that the covenant was with their leaders, and that the description applies to anyone who shows these traits. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan consider that the phrase may refer to disbelieving allies who break their word, and that it covers anyone who combines these qualities. Most exegetes understand the word dawabb as covering every creature that moves, humans included, whereas al-Sha'rawi holds that ordinary usage limits the term to four-legged animals, so the comparison concerns acting without reason. Al-Zamakhshari sees a gradation of evil: the disbeliever, then the one who persists, then the one who breaks covenants. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the lack of God-consciousness is firmly rooted in them. The following verses command that these enemies be dealt with severely so as to serve as a warning, that a treaty be openly annulled if treachery is feared, and that strength be prepared. The commentators present these views without deciding between them.

This verse states that the worst creatures in God's sight are those who persist in disbelief and will never believe. The commentators identify them first with the Jews of Banu Qurayza, with whom the Prophet had made a covenant not to fight him or aid his enemies. They armed the Meccans, claimed they had forgotten and made a mistake, then broke a second pact during the Battle of the Trench. Al-Tabari, Mujahid, Ibn Abbas and Ibn Kathir report this account, to which al-Baghawi adds Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf's role in Mecca. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan say the verse applies to anyone with this conduct until the Day of Resurrection, while al-Alusi and Ibn Ashur think it may also target other polytheist tribes and especially the hypocrites, Ibn Ashur suggesting it was revealed after Badr.

Grammarians differ on the word "min" in "from among them": partitive for those who note that only leaders made covenants, a mere emphasis, or the sense of "with" for others. On "they do not fear", some understand it as fearing shame and the Fire, others as fearing God when breaking the pact.

The verse also sets a line of conduct toward such traitors: to strike them firmly so that those behind them are scattered and take warning. Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatada are cited on this, and Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di draw the lesson that punishment deters, Ibn Sa'di adding that it is not permitted to betray a pledge given to a disbeliever. Ibn Kathir also cites the rule of openly announcing the end of a treaty when treachery is feared, reported by Abu Dawud.

This verse, as the commentators explain it, tells the Prophet ﷺ that if he gains the upper hand in battle over those who broke their covenant, who are for most scholars the Banu Qurayza, he must inflict a punishment severe enough to scatter those behind them and deter them from doing the same. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan and Muqatil take tashrid to mean punishment, warning and dispersal, while al-Tabari recalls its basic sense of driving off and scattering. Abu 'Ubayda and al-Qutaybi take it as making the news spread so that others hear of it. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya understand those 'behind them' as enemies who will follow the same path, not only those present. The reading of Ibn Mas'ud, 'fashharrid' with a dhal, is considered rare by al-Mahdawi, who sees it as a substitution of the dal, while al-Zamakhshari links it to the root shadhar. Mujahid holds that the following verse, about fear of treachery and the duty to announce the termination of a treaty openly, concerns the Banu Qurayza, whereas Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Kathir apply it to the future. The scholars agree that the aim is to deter the enemy from breaking its pledges, and that God does not love traitors.

God instructs His Prophet ﷺ that if he fears treachery from a people with whom he has a covenant, and signs of that treachery have appeared, he should openly cancel the covenant and inform them of it, so that he and they stand on equal footing in knowing it is void, avoiding both the charge of betrayal and a surprise attack. Most commentators, following Mujahid, say the verse was revealed concerning the Banu Qurayza. Ibn 'Atiyya argues that the Qurayza affair ends with the preceding verse and that this one addresses a general future case, a people whose treachery is feared but not yet proven. Many therefore distinguish two situations: when signs of treachery are only suspected, the enemy must be notified; when treachery is certain and clearly manifest, as when the Prophet marched on Mecca at the conquest, no formal renunciation is needed. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi cite the hadith of Sulaym ibn 'Amir, transmitted through 'Amr ibn 'Abasa, that one must neither loosen nor tighten a pact before its term without announcing its end 'on equal terms'. On the phrase 'ala sawa', the commentators differ: equality in knowledge of the breach, according to al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi; a respite, according to al-Walid ibn Muslim, which al-Tabari rejects as unsupported by Arabic usage; justice or equity for others; or openness, meaning a public announcement. The verse closes with God not loving traitors, which some read as a warning against attacking before announcing the breach and others as encouragement to fight once it has been announced.

This verse tells the Prophet ﷺ and the believers not to suppose that those who disbelieved have escaped, for they cannot outrun or escape God. The commentators differ on how to read it. Most readers use the second person, and al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that the idolaters who fled at Badr will not escape God's punishment. Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan mainly see it as a consolation to the Prophet and the believers about those who got away. The third-person reading has been defended by Ibn Atiyya, Abu Ali al-Farisi and al-Razi, who justify it by an implied object or by the presence of an implied

This verse commands the believers to prepare against their enemies whatever force they can muster, including horses kept ready for battle, so that they strike fear into the enemy of God and their own enemy, and into others they do not know but God knows. The commentators read this as a deterrent: an enemy who sees a strong Muslim army will not dare attack it. They agree that force covers any weapon or equipment useful in war, and that the mention of horses highlights their importance. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others cite the hadith of 'Uqba ibn 'Amir, 'Indeed, strength is archery', while Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi argue that this does not exclude other means and that archery was the greatest strength of that age. On the horses, 'Ikrima took the males as the strength and the females as the tethered mounts, whereas most scholars take the term generally for both. On the 'others you do not know', Mujahid named the Banu Qurayza, al-Suddi the Persians, Ibn Zayd and al-Hasan the hypocrites, and al-Tabari the jinn, while Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan favour the hypocrites. The verse closes with the promise that whatever is spent in God's cause will be repaid in full, in this world and the next according to Ibn Kathir.

This verse says that if the enemy inclines toward peace and an end to fighting, the Prophet should incline to it as well, and place his trust in God, who hears and knows all. The commentators agree on the apparent meaning: a leaning toward peace, truce or reconciliation. They differ, however, on how the verse applies. Al-Tabari holds that it concerns peace with the People of the Book who agree to pay the jizya, and that the verse is not abrogated by the verses of repentance (al-Tawba), since each remains valid for its own case. Ibn Kathir takes a similar line, holding that a truce is permitted when the enemy is numerous. Qatada, al-Hasan, 'Ikrima and Ibn Zayd consider it abrogated by the fighting verses of Surat al-Tawba, and Ibn 'Abbas links it to the verse in Surat Muhammad forbidding weakness and calls for peace while you are the stronger. Al-Suddi and Ibn Ishaq read it as an invitation to accept peace if the enemy asks for Islam. Mujahid attributes it to the Banu Qurayza. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi hold that the matter rests with the ruler, according to what serves Islam and its people: peace is neither compulsory nor permanent. Al-Razi regards the verse as not abrogated and sees in it an order to make peace when it is beneficial. The jurists quoted by al-Qurtubi generally set the length of a truce at around ten years, following the example of Hudaybiyya.

This verse reassures the Prophet ﷺ: if the enemies pretend to want peace while hiding treachery, God is sufficient for him, as He already supported him with victory at Badr and with the believers. The commentators agree that this support is a divine victory and that the believers mean the Emigrants and the Helpers, although al-Tabari, al-Sudi and Ibn 'Atiyya stress the Helpers in particular. As for the intended deception, Mujahid and Ibn Ishaq identify the Banu Qurayza, while Muqatil describes the Jews of Qurayza allied with the polytheists. The preceding verse, which commands accepting peace, is disputed: Qatada, al-Hasan and Ibn 'Abbas hold it abrogated by the verse of the sword, whereas al-Tabari, al-Nahhas and Ibn Kathir deny any abrogation, saying peace remains permissible depending on circumstances or for the People of the Book. The other major point concerns the joining of hearts: most exegetes take it to mean the reconciliation of the Aws and Khazraj, long-standing enemies, through Islam, and al-Razi sees in it proof of God's direct action on hearts. Ibn Mas'ud and Mujahid extend it to those who love one another for God's sake, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya keep a general sense. Nearly all agree that such unity is a miracle that no human effort, not even spending all the earth's wealth, could achieve.

The commentators explain that the verse reminds the Prophet ﷺ of God's favour: He supported him with His help and with the believers, and He joined their hearts after they had been divided. Most, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baydawi, take this to refer to the Aws and the Khazraj, who had fought for long years in pre-Islamic times and became brothers and helpers through Islam. All agree that such unity cannot be bought with any amount of wealth, since hearts belong to God, who turns them as He wills; al-Zamakhshari and al-Alusi present it as a manifest sign of prophethood. Ibn Mas'ud and others report that it concerns those who love one another for God's sake, and Ibn 'Atiyya notes that this may extend to all believers, Emigrants and Helpers, as a fine illustration rather than a cause of revelation. On the preceding verse, 'if they incline to peace', scholars differ: Qatada, al-Hasan and Ibn 'Abbas hold it abrogated by the sword verse in Surat al-Tawba, while al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir consider it not abrogated, applying to the People of the Book or to a truce when Muslims are weak. Al-Mawardi lists three meanings of 'peace'. For the closing 'Mighty, Wise', the common reading is that God prevails over His command and that His wisdom governs His acts. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi use the verse to support the view that states of the heart are created by God, a position the Mu'tazilites contest, seeing the union as a divine grace.

In this verse God addresses His Prophet ﷺ to reassure him and the believers who follow him: God is sufficient for them against their enemies, so they should not be dismayed by the enemy's numbers or by their own small number. Most commentators understand it as: God is sufficient for you, and for those believers who follow you, the word 'man' being in the accusative and coordinated with the pronoun in 'hasbuka'. This is the view of al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Juzayy, and of al-Sha'bi and Ibn Zayd, and al-Zamakhshari supports it with the well-known line 'fa-hasbuka wa al-Dahhak sayfun muhannad'. Al-Farra' and some grammarians read 'man' in the nominative, coordinated with the divine name: God suffices you, and so do the believers, a view favoured by al-Kisa'i. Ibn al-Qayyim and al-Shanqiti hold that sufficiency belongs to God alone, and they prefer the reading that keeps it exclusive to Him, citing the Qur'anic distinction between sufficiency and support. Abu Hayyan judges that an implied 'wa hasb' is the best reading, while Ibn Ashur sees the verse as a preface to the commands about fighting. Accounts of the occasion of revelation also differ: according to al-Kalbi and others it was sent down at al-Bayda' during the battle of Badr before the fighting began, while Ibn Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr link it to the conversion of 'Umar, which brought the believers to forty; Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan question that report. Ibn Sa'di stresses that divine sufficiency depends on faith and following the Prophet, and al-Qurtubi notes the general scope of the verse.

The verse orders the Prophet ﷺ to urge the believers to fight, and gives them the good news that twenty steadfast men will overcome two hundred unbelievers, and a hundred steadfast men will overcome a thousand, because the unbelievers are a people who do not understand, meaning they fight without seeking reward or hoping for God's recompense, and do not hold firm when the believers face them. The commentators explain that although the sentence is in the form of a statement, its meaning is a command. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata', Mujahid, 'Ikrima and al-Dahhak report that the believers were first required not to flee from ten enemies, and then granted relief so that they need not flee from two. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Ibn Kathir treat this relief as an abrogation, whereas Makki ibn Abi Talib considers it a mere concession, like the permission to break the fast while travelling. Ibn 'Atiyya also calls it abrogation while acknowledging the debate, and Ibn al-Jawzi notes differing rulings. The readers differed on some vowelling, such as whether the verb is feminine or masculine and whether the word for weakness is pronounced with a fatha or a damma, but the scholars regard these variants as having the same meaning. Al-Razi and al-Nasafi explain that the unbeliever, who does not believe in the afterlife, clings to this world, while the believer, who hopes for reward, stands firmer. The verse also affirms that victory comes by God's permission and that God is with the steadfast.

The commentators explain that this verse came after an earlier command requiring each Muslim to stand against ten enemies. Because this was hard on the believers, God lightened it so that one must stand against two, and the verse adds that victory comes by God's permission and that God is with the patient. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Abu Hayyan note that the earlier verse was phrased as a statement but meant as a command, and that the relief followed a heavier burden; they cite a report from Ibn Abbas that a man was at first forbidden to flee from ten, and later from two. Most scholars therefore hold that this verse abrogated the earlier one. Makki ibn Abi Talib, as cited by Ibn Attiyya and Abu Hayyan, considers it a mere concession, like the permission to break the fast while travelling. Abu Muslim al-Isfahani, reported by al-Razi, denies any abrogation, linking the earlier ruling to the condition that the twenty be able to endure. Some scholars, according to Ibn Attiyya, held that standing against ten was a recommendation rather than an obligation. The readings differ on the vowel of the word for weakness, which most treat as having the same meaning, while some distinguish bodily weakness from weakness of judgment. Al-Zamakhshari explains the repetition of the ratios as showing that the situation is the same whether the numbers are small or large.

This verse was revealed after the Battle of Badr and rebukes the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ for accepting ransom for prisoners before they had thoroughly subdued the polytheists. The commentators explain "until he has inflicted a heavy toll in the land" as thorough slaughter and subjugation that humbles disbelief and strengthens Islam, while al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report the meaning as prevailing or being firmly established, according to other scholars. The "goods of this world" are the ransom money, so called because it is short-lived, whereas God desires the Hereafter, meaning what leads to it through exalting the religion.

The scholars broadly agree that the rebuke targets those who inclined toward ransom rather than the Prophet ﷺ himself, who followed Abu Bakr's advice; al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that Umar favoured execution and that Sa'd ibn Mu'adh preferred a heavy toll to sparing men. Ibn Ashur holds that the rebuke concerns preferring fleeting worldly advantage over the religion's lasting interest, and Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Atiyya read it as a reproach to the Companions' greed.

On the phrase "a prior decree from God", views differ: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and al-Hasan take it as God's earlier permission of booty for this community, others as God's forgiveness of the people of Badr, al-Zamakhshari as God not punishing error in judgement, and al-Qurtubi notes several more readings. The verse ends by commanding them to eat of the lawful and good spoils and to be mindful of God, who is forgiving and merciful. Ibn Abbas held that the prohibition belonged to the early period when Muslims were few, and some commentators take the later verse of Muhammad as abrogating or qualifying it.

This verse rebukes the believers after the battle of Badr for accepting ransom from the captured polytheists before the enemy had been decisively weakened. The phrase "had not a Book from God preceded" is read in several ways. Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Abu Hurayra, Ubayda and Ibn Ishaq understand it as God's decree, from eternity, making spoils and ransom lawful for this community, the reading al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir adopt and al-Qurtubi calls the most sound. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd take it as God's forgiveness of the people of Badr. Others read it as the principle that God does not punish someone for an act done in ignorance or before a prohibition is stated, or as the Qur'an itself, which forgives minor sins. Al-Tabari holds that all these meanings are included. The commentators report that 'Umar wanted the captives killed, Abu Bakr advised ransom, and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh said that heavy slaughter was dearer to him. The Prophet is quoted as saying that had a punishment descended, only 'Umar and Sa'd would have been spared. Ibn Atiyya, Ibn Juzayy and Ibn Ashur see the verse as rebuking the preference for worldly gain, and not the Prophet, who followed the majority. Al-Razi and al-Baydawi, answering objections about the prophets' infallibility, say an honest error in judgement can occur without being left uncorrected. Modern commentators such as Ibn Sa'di, Sayyid Qutb and al-Sha'rawi stress the lesson for military leadership and the principle that no punishment comes before a law.

This verse permits the believers to eat of the spoils they have taken, which is lawful and good, and tells them to be mindful of God, who is Forgiving and Merciful. The commentators read it as a continuation of the rebuke given just before it concerning the prisoners of Badr. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that the believers had held back from the ransom money until this verse came down. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu Hayyan explain that the particle fa signals a consequence of a permission left implicit, and that the word halal removes any scruple that remained in the hearts, while tayyib refers to what is wholesome and agreeable. On the meaning of 'what you have taken', Ibn 'Ashur and Abu al-Su'ud see the word ghanimtum as applying linguistically to the ransom, whereas others keep the term for booty in its strict legal sense. As for the 'prior Book' mentioned in the previous verse, al-Tabari gathers all its proposed meanings without choosing one, while Ibn Kathir notes that several early authorities understood it as God's prior decree making the spoils lawful for this community. The closing phrase, 'God is Forgiving and Merciful', is taken by most as the reason for the command to fear God, since He pardons what came before the permission to take ransom.

The verse addresses the Prophet ﷺ, telling him to say to the captives from Badr who are in the hands of the Muslims that if God knows there is goodness in their hearts, meaning sincere faith, He will give them something better than the ransom they paid and will forgive them. The commentators agree that the verse was revealed about the captives of Badr and that the goodness meant is faith. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report that al-Abbas, the Prophet's uncle, was among them and said the verse was revealed about him; he later said he received twenty slaves who traded with his money and hoped for forgiveness. Ibn Ishaq and others take the verse to concern al-Abbas alone, whereas a report from Ibn Abbas cited by al-Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi holds that it applies to all the captives. Al-Razi argues that the wording implies generality even if al-Abbas was the occasion. Opinions differ on the good that is promised: al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Atiyya understand it as worldly provision or reward in the afterlife, while al-Razi allows for both. Al-Zamakhshari and others note variant readings of the words for captives and for taking, which do not change the core meaning. As for the betrayal mentioned in the next verse, Ibn Atiyya and al-Baydawi link it to breaking a pledge or to feigning conversion and then returning to disbelief, while Qatada connects it to the case of Abd Allah ibn Abi Sarh; Ibn Atiyya considers that this event, which took place at the conquest of Mecca, cannot be the cause of the revelation.

This verse says that if the prisoners of Badr intend to betray the Prophet ﷺ after their release, they should know that they had already betrayed Allah through disbelief, and so Allah gave them into the hands of the believers at Badr. Allah is all-knowing and wise in how He repays them. The commentators generally take the pronoun in 'they intend' to refer to the prisoners, and understand betrayal in several ways. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain it as saying one thing outwardly while hiding another, and they read 'He gave them power over them' as the victory at Badr. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Abbas connect the verse to al-Abbas and his companions, while Qatada links it to Abd Allah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh; Ibn 'Atiyya considers the latter view mistaken, since Ibn Abi Sarh's story belongs to the conquest of Mecca. Al-Razi notes three meanings of betrayal: disbelief, refusing to pay the agreed ransom, and breaking the pledge made at release. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi understand it as reneging on the pledge of Islam and returning to the faith of the fathers. Al-Razi sees in the verse a promise to the Prophet that he will prevail over anyone who breaks his covenant. Al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud present it as both a warning and a reassurance: if the captives return to fighting, Allah will again deliver them. Ibn Juzayy and others link the verse to the story of al-Abbas, who paid his ransom and later spoke of the wealth he had left with his wife, accounts which al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir report at length.

This passage sets out the categories of believers in the time of the Prophet ﷺ and the rights each holds. The emigrants who left their homes and struggled with their wealth and persons, and the Ansar who sheltered and aided them, are allies of one another. The commentators agree that wilaya here means mutual support and aid, but al-Tabari, Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Hasan, Ikrima and al-Sudi also take it to mean the right of inheritance, later abrogated by the verse that blood relatives have closer claims in the Book of God. Abu Hanifa and Ahmad follow this reading, as Ibn Ashur reports. As for believers who did not emigrate, there is no wilaya between them and the emigrants until they migrate. If they ask for help in the matter of religion, it is obligatory to help them, except against a people bound by a treaty, whose covenant must not be broken. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari hold that this denial is not limited to inheritance but covers mutual support, and Ibn Kathir notes that non-emigrants receive no share of booty unless they fought. Some held that emigration ended with the conquest of Mecca, while al-Hasan Basri considered it continuing. The passage concludes that disbelievers are allies of one another, and that neglecting the duty of mutual support would bring discord and great corruption. God is seeing of what you do.

This verse states that those who disbelieve support one another and form alliances among themselves, and it calls on believers to do the same among themselves. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and most commentators understand it as mutual support, aid and solidarity. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Ishaq and others read it as a rule of inheritance: believers inherited from one another (emigrants and helpers), while disbelievers inherited among themselves, and Muslims did not inherit from non-Muslims. This reading relies on a hadith transmitted from Usama ibn Zayd that a Muslim does not inherit from a disbeliever nor a disbeliever from a Muslim. Al-Tabari nonetheless prefers the sense of support, since the word wali in Arabic primarily means helper, while inheritance is a more distant meaning. As for the phrase 'if you do not do it', commentators differ on whether it refers to solidarity, to inheritance or to keeping the covenant. Most explain fitna as the strengthening of disbelief and the weakening of Islam, while Ibn 'Atiyya understands it as the trial of war and its consequences, and great corruption as the spread of polytheism. Al-Razi and Ibn 'Ashur note that mixing believers with polytheists, when the former were recent converts, risked drawing them back to disbelief, and that a divided community was itself a great corruption.

This verse describes the complete believers among the Emigrants and the Helpers: those who emigrated and struggled in God's cause, and those who sheltered and supported the Prophet and the Emigrants. They are truly believers, and they receive forgiveness, which al-Tabari explains as God's veil over their sins, and a generous provision, which the commentators understand as the provision of Paradise, free of any impurity. Al-Tabari cites a hadith in Sahih Muslim that the food of Paradise becomes a fragrant sweat like musk. Most commentators read the verse as praise and a testimony to the sincerity of the faith of both groups. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi argue that the repetition of the formula is not a true duplication but serves to exalt their station and to set out several grounds of praise. Al-Razi and al-Sam'ani also note that the Emigrants were of different ranks, so the first mention refers to the early emigration and the second to the later one. Regarding the mutual bond stated in the surrounding verses, Ibn Abbas, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir take it as a right of inheritance based on emigration, later abrogated by the verse on blood relatives. Al-Tabari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi understand it instead as mutual aid and support rather than inheritance. Legal debates, such as the inheritance of distant relatives, are mainly treated in the commentary on the following verse, where al-Qurtubi reports the views of Malik, Abu Hanifa and al-Shafi'i.

This verse states that those who believed after the first believers, emigrated and fought alongside the Muslims, belong to them, with the same rights and duties. Ibn 'Abbas says these are those who emigrated after the Treaty of Hudaybiya, called the second emigration; others say after the revelation of this passage or after Badr, and al-Razi holds that they are those who emigrated after the first emigration. The second part, that blood relatives are closer to one another 'in the Book of God,' is understood by most commentators as abrogating the inheritance that was based on emigration, alliance, or brotherhood, in favour of kinship. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan and Qatada hold that the verse covers all kin, while al-Tabari and al-Zamakhshari take the 'Book' to mean God's decree, the preserved tablet, or the Qur'an. Jurists differ on whether distant relatives inherit: Abu Hanifa and his followers cite this verse to give them a share, whereas Malik and al-Shafi'i reject this or restrict it. Al-Shinqiti concludes, on the basis of hadiths, that the maternal uncle inherits when there is no other heir. Ibn 'Ashur reads the verse as offering a way back for those who delayed emigrating, without judging between the schools. The verse closes by stating that God knows everything, meaning that He knows what suits His servants.
